newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian opposition pledge to defy demo ban.
newsitem.headline: Albanian opposition pledge to defy demo ban.

text.p: Albanian's main opposition parties pledged to defy a government ban and rally in the centre of Tirana on Saturday to protest against the dramatic failure of pyramid investment funds.

In the southern city of Vlore, tens of thousands of people took to the streets for a fourth day, demanding the resignation of the right-wing government and the return of their life savings, swallowed by the collapsed pyramid schemes.

The Interior Ministry turned down an opposition request to hold a similar demonstration in the heart of the capital between noon and 2 p.m. (1100-1300 GMT) on Saturday, arguing that such a protest posed a security risk.
An alliance of main opposition groups, the Forum for Democracy, set up last week in a cross-party bid to oust the ruling Democratic Party, pronounced the ban illegal.
"In such a situation, the Forum...calls on citizens to attend a large rally to protest against the government's irresponsibility," the Forum said in a statement.
Widespread riots swept Albania last month in an initial upsurge of anger against the collapsing pyramid schemes.

Hours before Saturday's demonstration was due to start, large numbers of policemen, some armed with automatic weapons, stood guard around Tirana's large Skanderbeg Square. Some reporters were cleared from the area.
"We can't assume any responsibilty for what might happen later," a policeman told Reuter correspondent Llazar Semini.
A convoy of cars driven by Democratic Party supporters swept through the wide, dusty square, which still bears the scars of rioting there two weeks ago, blaring their horns.
Bystanders in the streets bustling with hawkers and pavement stalls ignored them.
A swift police crackdown and a string of arrests following January's disturbances seemed to deter people from holding further protests for a time.

But the protests resumed this week. Crowds streamed through the streets of Vlore each day following the demise of a local fund. More than 20,000 people marched on Saturday, led by women waving bouquets of plastic flowers.

The crowd's numbers were swelled by students from local schools who quit their classes to join the procession, chanting slogans calling for the resignation of President Sali Berisha, founder of the Democratic Party.
"Today Tirana will be like Vlore," Albania's top selling daily Koha Jone said in a banner front page headline.

But it was uncertain whether people in Tirana would defy the interior ministry ban. Police moved swiftly to break up protests called in the capital last week, herding people off the roads and making a number of arrests. ty, in a statement broadcast on state television, warned Albanians against what it termed "the red terror" being organised by the main opposition Socialist Party.
"The Democratic Party calls on all citizens not to blindly follow forces aiming to create a drama many times worse than that of the pyramid schemes," it said.

The Democrats won re-election last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers. Some opposition politicians accuse the party of financing the victory with proceeds from the failed pyramid companies.
